assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theory-led prediction (flat bands at a magic twist angle) followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials. It is a clear case of a new platform for correlated states that theory anticipated and measurement confirmed, and it connects naturally to first-principles and continuum-model band theory I know well. It echoes how 2D carbon surprised us in 2010.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model supplies the prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive 2018 experiments. The credited trio is a workable configuration, though the experimental credit is shared with the early-career researchers who led the measurements, and the theory credit with others who studied moire bands before 2011.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many groups and platforms (twisted multilayers, TMDs) in under a decade; the phenomenology is stable even though the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated.
uncertainties: The microscopic origin of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved.
Credit among the experimental team and earlier theorists of twisted-bilayer band structure is not fully settled.
Whether the field is mature enough for recognition versus still rapidly evolving.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions (1995) and the later giant effect in crystalline MgO barriers underlie modern hard-disk read heads and MRAM. It is a physical discovery in spin-dependent tunnelling with enormous technological use, and band-structure theory (spin-filtering by symmetry of Bloch states) explains the MgO enhancement quantitatively, which I value.
assessment.attribution: Moodera and Miyazaki independently reported reproducible room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and the Yuasa/Djayaprawira groups achieved the MgO giant TMR. Julliere's earlier low-temperature work and the MgO theory (Butler, Mathon) fall outside the credited names, and the exact three-way allocation is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Over two decades of independent confirmation and commercial deployment; the interpretation is stable and recognition is, if anything, overdue relative to the 2007 GMR prize.
uncertainties: Who deserves the MgO-barrier credit (Parkin versus Yuasa and others, or the theorists) is not captured by the credited list.
Risk that the committee views it as an incremental extension of the GMR prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, with the HgTe experimental observation of helical edge transport, established a new state of matter classified by topology and spawned the field of topological materials. It is a textbook example of theory-experiment synergy.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contribution; Molenkamp's group did the experimental confirmation in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and 3D topological insulators involve further contributors (Fu, Moore, Hasan). A fair configuration is plausible but contentious, and that is a real concern.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups, with ARPES and transport on 2D and 3D materials; mature and widely recognised, though practical impact remains limited.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers (Fu, Kane, Mele, Hasan, Moore) complicate attribution.
Quantization of edge transport in HgTe is less precise than in the quantum Hall effect, which is a lingering concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a controlled non-perturbative treatment of strongly correlated electrons (Mott transition, heavy fermions) and, combined with DFT, underlies realistic calculations of correlated materials. This is exactly the bridge between first-principles theory and spectra that I care about, and it is a deep, original theoretical advance.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar mapped it to an impurity problem, and Muller-Hartmann and others contributed; the credited trio is defensible but leaves out Metzner and others, and the allocation is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use and validation against spectroscopy and cold-atom experiments; mature, though the validity in low dimensions and the quantitative accuracy of DFT+DMFT are still debated.
uncertainties: Omission of Walter Metzner and other early contributors from the credited names.
As a method, rather than a single physical discovery, it may be judged less decisive for a prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third class of collinear magnetism with compensated order yet spin-split bands, predicted from symmetry and ab initio calculations and confirmed by spectroscopy. It is directly in my own research area, with potential for spintronics and a clear, original conceptual step.
assessment.attribution: The symmetry classification and the first-principles predictions are credited to Šmejkal, Jungwirth, Sinova and collaborators; credit would need care relative to earlier spin-group work (Yuan, Hayami, Naka and others) and the ARPES/MnTe experimental teams.
assessment.maturity: Very recent (c. 2019-2022 onward), with ARPES and other confirmations in MnTe and CrSb but a young literature; probably premature as a prize at this time, though promising.
uncertainties: Maturity and independence of experimental confirmation are still developing.
Priority questions with earlier spin-group symmetry papers by other authors.
Possible conflict of interest in my judgement because the topic is close to my own work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of the skyrmion lattice in chiral magnets (MnSi) and its real-space imaging, along with emergent electrodynamics and the topological Hall effect, reveals a new topologically protected magnetic texture and has been tied to spin-transfer torque control. It combines neutron scattering, theory and microscopy in a way I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group provided the neutron discovery (with Boni and others), Tokura's group the Lorentz-microscopy real-space observation, and Rosch the theory of emergent fields; Bogdanov's earlier prediction is a significant omission from the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups, though room-temperature applications are still developing; the physics is mature while the technology has not matured.
uncertainties: Bogdanov's early theoretical prediction is not in the credited list.
Potential for the committee to view practical impact as insufficiently demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High-resolution ARPES transformed the direct measurement of band structure, Fermi surfaces, gaps and many-body renormalisation in cuprates and other correlated materials, a prime link between experiment and theory. It is an instrument-plus-discovery contribution of broad importance in solid-state physics.
assessment.attribution: Shen and Campuzano are widely identified as leaders in applying high-resolution ARPES to the cuprates, but it is a technique developed by many, including synchrotron and detector developers, and the two names may not capture the whole community. A two-person prize is possible but not clean.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced over three decades; the technique is mainstream, though specific physical discoveries (pseudogap, kinks) remain debated.
uncertainties: Whether this is a technique recognition or a discovery recognition.
Omission of earlier ARPES developers and other cuprate-spectroscopy groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller proposed trapped-ion quantum gates and also foundational proposals for quantum simulation with cold atoms, shaping the whole field of programmable quantum matter. The importance and lasting impact are very high, and it connects to correlated many-body physics I follow, though I defer somewhat in AMO matters.
assessment.attribution: The two-person configuration is natural for the theoretical foundations; the experimental realisations (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others) are credited elsewhere and Wineland already received the 2012 prize, so the attribution must be framed carefully as theory.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally validated over decades in trapped ions and neutral atoms; the timing is mature, and recent hardware progress strengthens it.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) and with other quantum-simulation candidates.
I have limited expertise to judge the priority claims in AMO theory.
